  "candidates": [
    {
      "startEvent": 657,
      "endEvent": 672,
      "contextStartEvent": 610,
      "contextEndEvent": 785,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "is the message driving people away from, you know, true theology about Jesus.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "Horn restricts competing theological miracles to overlooked natural causes or malevolent supernatural causes, then tests them against already accepted theology (E657–672). This protects that theology from contrary miracle evidence without independently establishing the diagnostic test. It is an explanatory argument, not a catchphrase; he also supplies specific natural explanations and acknowledges insufficient Christian evidence (E637–639, E673–785)."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2573,
      "endEvent": 2581,
      "contextStartEvent": 2562,
      "contextEndEvent": 2618,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "if I was the devil, I'd want to make a religion",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "After renewed discussion of Whitmer's retained testimony, Horn again offers natural or demonic explanations (E2573–2581). Doctrinal disagreement supplies the proposed demonic motive, potentially absorbing contrary miracle evidence. However, the explicitly hypothetical wording offers a possible explanation rather than declaring every rival result defeated; its protective force beyond the earlier episode remains uncertain."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2613,
      "endEvent": 2618,
      "contextStartEvent": 2562,
      "contextEndEvent": 2618,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "I'm going to believe God over Whitmer",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity", "shame"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The affirmation privileges God over a witness and connects allegedly contradictory revelations to defective character (E2610–2618). It could shield accepted theology by presupposing which testimony represents God. However, Horn supplies an ordinary credibility reason—apparent inconsistency—and O'Connor distinguishes rejecting a church from rejecting its original vision (E2582–2609); unconditional protection or substituted reasoning is not established."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 1600,
      "endEvent": 1634,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "we want to establish uh the sincerity of testimony.",
      "explanation": "Horn explicitly limits persecution evidence to sincerity rather than proof of resurrection, then cites reported threats and suffering. This clarifies the inferential role of his earlier martyrdom argument (E1395–1461), without establishing that sincere testimony must be accurate."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2667,
      "endEvent": 2712,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "visions can be true.",
      "explanation": "O'Connor explains the distinction between visionary experience and false experience, illustrates it with Joseph's dream, and identifies firsthand testimony and specifically connected persecution as evidence that would strengthen the resurrection case. The repeated phrase summarizes a qualified argument rather than replacing one."
    }
  ]
